description.summary: A cursed wandering spirit of the Venezuelan and Colombian Llanos who carries his murdered father's bones in a sack and whose whistle reverses with distance: close-sounding when far, distant-sounding when very near.
description.full: El Silbón ('the whistler') is a legendary spirit of the Llanos region of Venezuela — particularly Portuguesa state and Guanarito Municipality — and of Colombia's Eastern Llanos, said to have arisen as a folk legend in the mid-19th century. According to the most widely told version, El Silbón was a spoiled son who, in a drunken rage, killed his father, and (in some versions) prepared the body as food for his unsuspecting mother; on discovering the truth, his grandfather whipped him, rubbed lemon and pepper into his wounds, and cursed him to wander forever, carrying his father's bones in a sack. He appears as the shadow of a tall, gaunt man, sometimes wearing a hat; in some accounts as a six-metre giant moving among the treetops. His characteristic whistle is held to be inverted in distance: when it sounds near, he is far; when it sounds faint and distant, he is dangerously close. He preys particularly on drunkards and unfaithful husbands. Folkloric protections include a barking dog (the only thing he reportedly fears), chili peppers, and a whip — items linked to the curse imposed by his grandfather.

etymology.origin: Spanish 'el silbón', literally 'the whistler' or 'the one who whistles', from the verb 'silbar' (to whistle).
etymology.first_use: Recorded in 19th-century Llanero oral tradition; widely standardised in 20th-century Venezuelan folkloric literature.

features.description: Most commonly described as the shadow of a tall, very thin man, sometimes in a hat
Carries a sack containing his father's bones, which he counts each night
Some Llanero accounts portray him as an enormous figure striding among the treetops
His whistle sounds close when he is far away, and faint when he is dangerously near

physical.morphology: Spectral; size and detail vary regionally between a man-shadow and a giant.

abilities.description: Distance perception of his whistle is reversed; the louder, the safer
Hearing his whistle is itself an omen of death; in some accounts he counts the bones at the sleeper's threshold
Held to be repelled by a barking dog, by chili pepper, and by the whip — items associated with his original curse

behavior.diet: Said to drink the blood of his victims and add their bones to his sack
patterns: Approaches lone, drunk, or unfaithful men at night
Whistles continually as he travels; the whistle is the principal phenomenological marker
Counts the bones in his sack each night

range.description: Folkloric range across the Llanos savanna of Venezuela and the Eastern Llanos of Colombia, with the densest tradition in the Venezuelan state of Portuguesa.

hotspots.name: Guanarito, Portuguesa
hotspots.notes: Region most strongly associated with the El Silbón legend in standard Venezuelan folklore.

peak_activity_periods.description: Period in which the legend is generally said to have arisen, per Wikipedia and Venezuelan folklore studies
Continued cultural prominence in Venezuelan and Colombian rural folk media

origins.cultural_roots: Llanero oral tradition of Venezuela and Colombia, fusing Iberian moral-tale conventions with regional Llanero rural cosmology and Catholic concepts of curse and unredeemed sin.
origins.earliest_accounts: Mid-19th-century oral tradition; recorded in 20th-century Venezuelan and Colombian folklore compilations.
origins.folklore_connections: Connected to a wider Hispanic-American complex of cursed-wanderer ghosts including La Llorona, El Sombrerón, La Sayona, La Patasola, and El Coco.

timeline.event: El Silbón legend takes shape in Venezuelan Llanero oral tradition (per Wikipedia)
Rómulo Gallegos publishes 'Cantaclaro', situating the Llanos in modern Venezuelan literary imagination and creating an audience for Llanero folklore
timeline.significance: Cultural context for 20th-century literary engagement with Llanero folklore

history.modern_era: El Silbón remains a vivid presence in Venezuelan and Colombian rural folklore, in school anthologies, in the 'joropo' musical tradition, and in popular culture (films, television, comics). The 2018 Venezuelan film 'El Silbón: Orígenes' and a sequel have given the figure renewed contemporary visibility.

paranormal.name: Cursed unredeemed soul
paranormal.description: El Silbón is the soul of a real or archetypal patricide condemned to wander forever as punishment, in keeping with Catholic and Llanero conceptions of the unredeemed dead.
evidence_cited: Apotropaic role of dogs and chilies tied directly to the curse story

skeptical.name: Moral-pedagogical folklore
skeptical.description: The legend functions as moral pedagogy and social control, warning especially against patricide, drunkenness, and infidelity in a rural Llanero context.

skeptical.name: Acoustic explanation of the inverted whistle
skeptical.description: The 'reversed' whistle motif may encode a real acoustic phenomenon of the open Llanos — sounds carry unevenly across the savanna at night, particularly with temperature inversions.
evidence_cited: Llanero familiarity with long-range acoustic effects in open savanna

folklore.beliefs: Hearing the whistle is itself an omen; if the whistle sounds close, no immediate danger; if it sounds far, the listener is in immediate peril. Protection is sought through dogs, chili pepper, and the whip.

literature: Llanero anthology stories in Venezuelan and Colombian school readers
El Silbón material in collected works of Venezuelan folklorists
games: Featured as a creature in Latin American indie horror games drawing on regional folklore
music: 'El Silbón' joropo songs in the Llanero musical tradition
other: Frequently invoked in Llanero rural pedagogy and as a regional cultural symbol
